title: What if I never had to navigate government again?
description: AI can do dramatically more than make government easier to navigate.
text:
Today I spent 3 hours at the DMV to update my license (on take 2 after I failed the vision test on take 1).

I’m also really late on this. I have not been a very proactive citizen following the rules because first I have to learn what the rules are, and learning what the rules are takes time.

You have to bring a bunch of documents apparently. First I went to the DC DMV website, figured out how to navigate to ‘License and ID’, then through a bunch of the tabs. Clicked around some more. I counted and it took 20 minutes to figure out what to bring, where to go, when they were open.

Then I had to figure out which documents I already had that met the requirements, print them out, and physically bring them to the DMV. Then they scanned my paper documents into a machine - because they had to be paper. Besides Saturdays, it is also only open *during* work hours, the exact times that most of us are working.

None of these individual steps are that hard, but the burden comes from me having to learn and navigate all of them. I have to know that I need to update my license. I have to find the right government website. I have to understand the rules. I have to figure out which rules apply to me. I have to find my paper documents. I have to move information between systems. I have to show up at the right office at the right time.

I, as a human, am the orchestration layer between a bunch of government systems and processes.

- - 

dmv.dc.gov

Alternatively, with a quick phrase, I could get all the information I needed in less than one minute with an AI chat tool, with links and all.

That already makes government dramatically easier to navigate. But what if we could do better? What if I didn’t need to spend 5 hours of my life doing this at all?

So what does good look like in the future?

Phase 1: AI helps me navigate government

Phase 2: AI navigates government for me.

Phase 3: Government anticipates what I need.

Phase 1: Make Government More Understandable

Clearly it looks much closer to immediate, personalized information delivered to me.

Where does that surface happen and is it something the government needs to own? Not exclusively.

What if government leaned into backend systems that made it easy to surface information in your favorite chat interface that already knows you & has access to your information? I just say ‘I need to update my license. What do I need to do?’

This basically already works today.

Phase 2: Make Government Operate Through Intent

Okay now I understand what I need to do faster - amazing. But I still have to print the documents out, go to the DMV, take (& fail) a vision test, come back with my prescription, and do it all over again.

But my chat interface also has access to my email, which is where my vision exam already is. It could have my license information and any other information I give it access to.

Instead I could just say ‘My residency is DC. Please fix whatever needs to happen.’

Software could figure out the process, pull in the information I’ve authorized it to access, and take whatever actions I allow it to take.

Now I’m no longer the human orchestration layer for the government.

Phase 3: Make Government Proactive

Okay, but what would need to happen to not have to do this at all?

What good could look like is that I’m in a new location - I get a notification that I should update my license. I’m asked if my information can be digitally pulled in, and then everything is verified digitally and automatically.

As always, there are some risks. The main one is perhaps increased fraud, as reducing friction can make fraud easier. Identity, authorization and security become increasingly important as software can do more for us. But we already apply for a lot of government services online and use strong identity verification. So this is mostly close to technically possible today.

Which gets to the bigger question -

Will we always need to build and maintain a dedicated frontend for every government service?

Government of course still needs to have excellent and accessible digital experiences. Websites are incredibly important to that in the near term. But over time, they increasingly may not be the primary way people interact with government.

Could we disconnect frontend and backend even more? Have amazing backend systems with the right APIs, MCPs, data models, permissions, business rules, and increasingly agent-accessible tools that allow us to take the relevant actions from our chat surface of choice?

In a former life, I spent a lot of time building “recommendation systems” - like when you go to tiktok or instagram and see your ordered posts, that’s what I did. The dream even then was all around - how can we understand what someone needs and surface it before they have to go looking for it?

We’re getting a lot closer to doing that with government services too.

And if I believe that to be true, what does that mean for actions we take now?

- Authoritative APIs and machine-readable rules

- Clean underlying data and shared definitions

- Strong digital identity and delegated authorization

- Secure transactional APIs, MCPs, and tools, not just information APIs

- Interoperability between government systems

- Services designed to be invoked by humans or software agents

In a post-2026 world, the government service itself can be more separable from the frontend we built for it. Government can provide its own website while also making it possible for people to interact with that same underlying service through other interfaces they choose.

I also really like the competition this creates on the frontend. Citizens aren’t locked into one website at all and have choice on the experience. Government still owns the authoritative service underneath it, but doesn’t need to own the ways someone interacts with it.

A digital form is just user interfaces that make humans fill in business rules.

Some predictions:

- Websites and forms become one of several digital methods of interacting with government.

- They don’t disappear, but now we’ve diversified from paper & in person, to phone calls, to static digital services, to much more flexible & personalized ways.

- Government backends become dramatically more important.

- APIs, data models, identity, permissions, business rules, and secure ways to take actions become the foundation.

- Government becomes proactive.

- If all goes well, it will just be awesome. The dream when I started in tech 10 years ago was how can we understand and solve needs before someone has to go looking for them? And we are getting there.

- Security becomes even more important.

- The more software can do for us, the more important security will become. Importantly, everything described here is feasible without further advances in AI technology.

I am excited for a world where we all navigate government a lot less in the first place.

title: AI Transformation: What Does Change Management Look Like When the Target Keeps Moving?
description: I didn’t grow up AI-native, but I did grow up digital-native.
text:
I didn’t grow up AI-native, but I did grow up digital-native. My father was a mechanical engineer who got my family a desktop computer before I was born. I spent my childhood learning BASIC and Visual Basic, making GeoCities pages, and HTMLing my Facebook page. So I didn’t need to learn that computers and the internet were clearly the ways that information should be stored, processed and exchanged.

I, along with most of the world, am still learning how to be AI-native though. Especially as what that phrase even means is rapidly evolving as technology continues to get better.

Lately I have been thinking a lot about how enterprises shift from ‘Digital Transformation’ to ‘AI Transformation’ - both the technology and the people parts of it. I’m already convinced AI is fundamentally changing how work happens. I’ve heard so many stories from a lawyer able to accomplish five times as much work with AI to  healthcare providers say constantly that they are able to spend more time on patients and clinical judgement, and less time on paperwork with AI. How do enterprises help hundreds of thousands of employees change how they work?

I think that most of the standard digital transformation change management practices still apply and are useful to lean into, but they are run as a much faster loop with multiple steps in parallel with AI. That is because every technology jump (which seems to happen monthly) reopens steps again (e.g., need to update vision with major new capabilities).

AI requires a change in rhythm in change management.

What is the Same Between Digital Transformation and AI Transformation?

The main way it is the same is both transformations represent a fundamental shift in how work happens. Employees were doing one thing and now they are doing a different thing.

What is Different?

1. The Destination is a Moving Target

In a traditional change management effort there is a clear before and after. Before you had paper health records and after you have a specific electronic health record. Paper records and electronic records require entirely different ways of working. It might be hard to get there, but you know where you are going so the destination can be the same throughout the change management project.

AI is continuing to increase in capability daily, so you have to continually update your ‘destination’.

2. AI Lowers the Cost of Experimentation

One reason AI changes the nature of transformation is that it isn’t just digitizing an existing process.

Traditional digital transformation automates workflows that humans already understand. But AI increasingly delegates parts of reasoning itself. Instead of programming ‘if X happens, do Y’, we ask AI to draft, summarize, prioritize, or reason within a set of guardrails.

Employees can often discover a dramatically better workflow for themselves in an afternoon simply by experimenting with AI capabilities, as opposed to organizations top-down prescribing the workflow updates.

This is kind of like AI democratizing digital transformation. It creates a more bottom-up approach because each individual or team can discover better ways of working for themselves, rather than waiting for a centrally designed process.

3. Highest Value Use Cases May Emerge Post Deployment

This one goes along with the previous one. There have been enough examples now across the world showing that the most effective ways of using AI often were surprises to the folks that created them, and not always in the original business case.

4. Capability Adoption Matters As Much as Technology Adoption

Due to all the above, AI transformation is clearly at least as much capability adoption as technology adoption. We must provide and teach the current AI technology, but the real focus will be teaching the capability to use the technology as it continues to evolve.

- - 

The Kotter Change Management Loop

Kotter’s Classic Eight Steps of Change Management

I was recently reading Kotter’s classic change management framework and thinking through how/if it applies to AI.

I don’t know what AI technology will look like two years from now - nobody does. So I think the standard 8 steps in change management still broadly apply, but there is a lot more iteration on all of them at once instead of an end-to-end pathway. We aren’t done with one change management cycle because we keep updating the destination.

For example,

- Vision (Step 3): A new AI capability means potentially revisiting the vision because employees can suddenly accomplish work that wasn’t previously possible. A new capability also requires new communications to update employee mental models of goals and possibilities. Training would continue to iterate with new capabilities as well.

- Volunteer Army (Step 4): Luckily I’ve found there are more than enough highly invested, early adopters signing up for the army - so this is more on channeling the volunteer energy in the right direction.

- Enabling Action By Removing Barriers (Step 5): From large organization perspective, the goal is to set high-level, clear guardrails for groups, as opposed to defining specific SOPs and detailed new, required ways of working.

- Generate Short Term Wins (Step 6): The most impactful wins come from the users experimenting and not a centrally controlled set of milestones, so it is more on encouraging and helping the wins proliferate than defining the wins beforehand.

Example: Software Engineering on 10x speed

I have watched this play out in software engineering over the past few years. Software AI started with autocomplete and line completion suggestions, which sped things up a bit. The next step was suggestions of whole chunks of functions, then being able to talk with your code, then updating many files at once, and now agents swarming to go from issue to code commit, etc. One change management cycle wouldn’t have gotten us here because there were rapid technology improvements and we didn’t know where we were going when we started.

Software engineering is also a bit of an edge case because software engineers are natural experimenters, but a similar pattern is coming for many other knowledge worker workflows.

Today, our tools allow people to draft, edit, review, delete, and iterate on documents. These are changes we want people to use because employees tell us they save time and improve their job satisfaction. The next step is that these may already be pre-drafted once we have the right data integrations and confidence in our systems.

Success in the In-Between Times

Success in digital transformation change management is how cleanly it can turn off a manual process and turn on a digital one. Success in AI transformation change management is much more iterative because we are living in the In-Between Times. First it looks like everyone experimenting. Then it looks like continuing to gain confidence in the tools. Then it looks more like handing off non-critical, administrative aspects of one’s work. It will be an iterative loop as AI continues to become more competent and humans continue to gain trust. We must train our workforces live during the transition.

The partnership of humans and AI systems will keep evolving as what each is best at keeps evolving. Implementing and teaching the AI tools of today is only part of the journey. Running the continuous change management loop will also be core to any enterprise’s AI transformation success.

*How do I use AI in writing? My personal approach is to write the whole draft manually, then I ask AI to rate it across a range of dimensions and for suggestions on how to improve it. Sometimes I take the suggestions.

**Why write at all? Writing is my favorite mode of communication. Like the Amazon 6-pager memo concept, I find that writing process forces the clarity of thinking and strategy in a way that other modes do not.

title: The AI-enabled enterprise will not be built from scratch.
text:
Start-ups are going AI-native and I’m a little jealous. A new company can get started faster than ever before leveraging AI tools for marketing, operations, coding, and even idea generation (examples, more examples). Midjourney started profitable with just 11 people and now does around $500M with roughly 110 people, which is about $4.7M per employee, a number that would have been science fiction five years ago. Garry Tan’s (Y Combinator President) set-up creates a set of agents that each fill a different role (CEO/CTO/COO for example) to lead, develop and run a company. More accessible no-code horizontal and vertical tools are rapidly emerging to open this up to anybody. Like the internet and mobile phones before it, AI expands what a single human or organization is capable of. It’s empowering.

But large organizations are not start-ups. They have a lot of legacy technology, processes, and regulations already running massive amounts of work. They don’t need more systems or even necessarily more migrations.

The second challenge is AI is still rapidly evolving, so enterprises that lock in a particular tech stack right now risk picking the wrong one and being locked into what could be another legacy technology a year from now.

So what do you do? How do you lean in considering how fast everything is moving and the legacy systems that currently exist?

I think the key ways to lean in are to make your current systems more accessible, to stay flexible on the specific AI tooling, and to let AI become the new connective tissue across all of those systems. This will bring the most near-term value, while preserving flexibility for the future. There are the 4 key layers (plus security infused throughout), but they all look a little different than they did even a year ago as AI platform capabilities continue to evolve.

- - 

Figure 1: An extremely AI-generated image showing new core AI capability as the connective tissue across systems.

Data Layer

As detailed here, centralized data platforms and storage still have their place, but I believe in decreased emphasis on perfectly structured data and on having all the data in one place. LLMs are very good at making sense of messy data, as long as they can safely access it. This gets at the overall approach - legacy systems don’t have to be fully consolidated or replaced - they need to be accessible. As long as AI can safely access your HR, ops, budget, etc. data, as well as lineage and metadata information on where it came from, AI is pretty good at making sense of it and serving as the connective tissue across systems. Therefore, the strategy should focus on making data discoverable, accessible, permissioned and usable by people and AI tools.

AI Layer: Or Is All Software Just One Software?

This is the layer that people most interact with, and also the layer that is evolving the fastest.

Recent tools have signaled a big shift in moving from text/image processing to no-code agents that can run on schedules, web extensions that can navigate websites, and long running parallel agents that can interact and evolve complex tasks. This means that by using just one of these general use tools, a complex task like Referral Management could be accomplished by autonomously navigating websites for referral information, securely storing relevant information in databases or sheets, pulling data from MCPs from a wide range of sources, and sharing the process with the relevant people. And instead of a custom bespoke application created by a software development team, all of these things are now feasible in highly accessible no-code applications.

This is a huge shift. I’ve heard the adage ‘Is all software just ephemeral and on-demand?’ but also  ‘Is all software just one software?’ I expect this to dramatically cut down on the amount of bespoke applications an organization needs to build or buy at all.

Governance

I see this layer lagging a bit behind the prior layer.

AI governance of one year ago was focused on deep evaluation of specific use cases, but the pace that new AI applications can be developed today demands a different approach. How can I ensure this referral management system I just built with no-code in an hour in a general-use platform actually works and is good enough to share and scale?

Right now, AI agent governance platforms are currently mostly separate bespoke products from the AI layer above. This creates a problem and a need to purchase from a 3rd party or a second product that may lag behind or deviate as they are not directly connected.

Over the next year, I hope that we see a stronger convergence of AI governance and agentic AI creation platforms - as it will be most effective for these to occur in the same place to allow simple, technical governance controls to ensure that applications are safe & reliable, but can also get out quickly.

Training & Enablement

The best training starts from real problems an organization has and shows staff how to solve them on their own in a no-code way - empowering staff to move more quickly and autonomously.

Luckily, from my experience, there is no shortage of staff interest in training or adoption - meaning there is generally very strong interest from staff in adopting AI tools and learning how to use them better (unlike electronic health records or other past technology that required literal regulation to get people to use them). There is both a need for broad training on the features, basic functions, and how to not generate AI slop, as well as domain specific training. Many folks think they are AI-enabled because they’ve replace web search with AI or they use it to plan their vacations - but I have found enablement sessions crucial to expanding the types of work AI can assist with dramatically. The most effective training I’ve seen is domain-specific, giving groups new tools to solve their own business objectives and creating the community venues for them to organically exchange knowledge and ideas.

So what do you do?

Those are the layers - but what do you do first? I believe in focusing on access and enablement, with the right guardrails. Getting people experimenting as much and as early as possible help organizations understand the highest value ways AI can help the organization and it creates a diaspora of early adopters that serve as force multipliers as additional capability, data connections, and governance are rolled out.

The other key thing is that AI is continuing to evolve so quickly, so even if all of the above were executed perfectly today, it would likely be outdated in a few months. This has to be an iterative operating model and not a one time build or upgrade.

Like buying a new car, the minute an AI stack gets put in place it starts to depreciate in value. Even more so than software development, the key to implementing the layers above is to be extremely flexible. This means creating data that is easy to access by the approved users, AI as the overall connective tissue, flexible governance, and training & enablement that focuses on end users solving their own problems with technology. It also means you shouldn’t buy AI like a car or a building - but focus on leasing and preserving optionality.

I’m still a little jealous of start-ups - but enterprises have their own advantages that they already execute massive projects, along with extensive institutional knowledge and scaled systems. I think that enterprise adoption through this approach allows enterprises to leverage the strong foundation they already have and to use that foundation in a fundamentally different way.

*How do I use AI in writing? My personal approach is to write the whole draft manually, then I ask AI to rate it across a range of dimensions and for suggestions on how to improve it. Sometimes I take the suggestions.

**Why write at all? Writing is my favorite mode of communication. Like the Amazon 6-pager memo concept, I find that writing process forces the clarity of thinking and strategy in a way that other modes do not.

title: Can AI Sell My Things for me?
description: It is on its way, but more access to systems and knowledge about my life would help.
text:
I’ve been testing whether and what is ready for prime-time in AI and useful in my daily life.

Some of the most useful personal workflows include: daily news briefs, weekly scan across messaging platforms on things to respond to, and my personal avatar twin with AI-generated voice, video and text. It is useful to understand what is possible, what isn’t quite there yet, and what I should immediately be adopting.

Recently, I was doing some spring cleaning and discovered I own too many things. I set one of the major agent workflow platforms to the task of selling them - a relatively complex task, only partially AI-ifyable at the moment since I didn’t use AI outside of my computer or computer vision based robots.

Objective: Sell unneeded items.

I really had to do the set-up myself, as the AI didn’t know I had these items and couldn’t predict which specific things I no longer wanted to own. (I could imagine a future where it is different: 1. It knows I like minimalism and that it’s spring; 2. I’ve already somehow cataloged my things whether with full pictures of my house or some pin I wear around that logs what I see. 3. Maybe one day I just act on AI’s priority suggestions.)

But for today, I came up with the list to sell and AI jumped in at that point. It first suggested routes of where to sell each thing (Facebook Marketplace vs. Nextdoor vs. Reverb for a guitar vs. a specialty store for a motorcycle jacket). Based just on the images, it suggested which items to post on which sites and created the proposed titles, images, and descriptions. It got close to auto-posting on each site, with human in the loop, though the Chrome extension AI-based RPA was very slow, about 6 mins per posting and all the sites have terms of service banning bot posting, which the AI wouldn’t try to get around. It really wasn’t much faster than doing it myself, but I could imagine a world where it is.

- - 

Figure 1: AI Created Spring Cleaning Sale Tracker

A few other observations:

- It created a shared tracker I could share with my husband, so he could manually add anything he sold (he wasn’t using AI for that part).

- Coordinating across platforms was clunky and the safety controls often had me affirmatively agree to actions in a way some other platforms would not have required.

- Deleting posts and information could be done more rapidly and fully autonomously.

- Scheduling time for someone to stop by worked well once I gave it some availability windows.

- Sometimes I just got in the way. I changed my mind on what to sell or didn’t feel like meeting someone. The AI just didn’t have these insights.

- Integrations were the biggest challenge. On Facebook Marketplace, most messages come in via Messenger, and the AI only had access to those through the slow Chrome extension with computer use. Separately navigating the webpage and messages of each website, without APIs was clunky, slow and could be finicky.

So did it help? 

Overall, yes - I’d estimate it saved ~5 hours through a few mechanisms: matching the right item to the right venue, the RPA post creation and the responses (though honestly for some of them I just sat on the couch and stared at it for a while, so I wasn’t making a good use of my increased time).

The barriers were mostly that computer use is still very slow and that I am impatient. And that this particular task was partially in the physical world.

I expect computer use to improve dramatically in the next year. And there are various ways AI could learn about the physical space, maybe I’ve already inventoried or photographed my place or maybe people will eventually have mini-robots.

It seems like the next phase will be technically much easier and faster than foundation model creation. It just needs three things:

- It has to be able to access things: It has to have easy and efficient interoperability. This isn’t novel and was true for software before AI as well. This is continuing to push on open systems and technical interoperability like APIs/MCPs.

- It has to know the state of the relevant world: The state of my house and the thoughts in my head were not accessible. We will continue to see ways from physical and software devices to ease data capture for AI systems.

- It has to be allowed to take action: This one is just a choice on what we allow AI to do vs. not do, not exactly a technology thing. And it will be an iterative process figuring out how to allow the right permissions at the right time.

So can AI sell my things for me? Yes, it can help substantially. It just also needs still needs me and my house to be a little bit involved.

title: How does Generative AI Change Data Platform Strategy?
description: Trying to reconcile platforms, copilots, and reality.
text:
I grew up in the ‘big data’ era. The 2010s saw digital data expand by 10x, 100x, 1000x.

I started in genomics, where the first digital genome was completed in 2002 and was around 200 GB. By 2010, there were thousands of genomes; by 2015 hundreds of thousands; by 2020 tens of millions. Meanwhile, in tech, the rise of social media resulted in LinkedIn (my first job) having 4 million members in 2005 to over 400 million in 2015.

Thanks for reading Kimberly’s Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

This was a lot of data and we believed it was the key to everything from understanding the root of human disease to outcompeting your social media competitors. To store and process all of it, we built new infrastructure: Hadoop, Spark, Hive, Redshift. These tools depended on data being centralized and reshaped into new formats. So organizations built massive, centralized data platforms in service of that mission.

And then, in 2022, we had another paradigm shift. Generative models arrived that were already very good and already pre-trained on domains as far apart as genomics and social media, and worked directly on unstructured data. Suddenly, it was technically feasible to just call something like client.responses.create(...) and bypass a lot of bespoke model training and data-platform plumbing.

So what does this mean for the future and role of centralized data platforms?

- - 

Hadoop elephant of yesterday and the copilots of today (Courtesy of ChatGPT.com. Clearly not my own artistic skills)

AI has moved some work to the “edge”

By “edge,” I mean close to the user and transactional system: a call-center app, an electronic health record, or an email client.

Before, “doing AI” usually meant: move data into a central store, engineer features, train a model, deploy it from the platform. Now, a whole class of things can be built as: base model + retrieval over your existing content + a simple UI + some guardrails.

Think: “chat with your documents” over policy PDFs, a copilot that summarizes emails or a tool that suggests marketing copy. These are judged mostly on: do people actually use this and like it? Is it safe enough? The focus is on user feedback and logging/monitoring what was done.

For these use cases, data accessibility matters more than centralization. The data has to be reachable via the right APIs (and increasingly MCP-style connectors), with identity and permissions enforced, just like any other modern web app feature.

So for that work, which is increasing, data strategy should focus on making data safely accessible where it already lives and logging the AI behavior, instead of ‘centralize first.’

Question one: do we need training at all?

The first question I ask now about a new AI idea is: do we actually need to train anything, or is prompt + retrieval enough?

If the job is mostly summarizing, drafting, or Q&A over existing text, and “good” is defined as time saved and user satisfaction, I’m usually happy to stay in prompt+RAG land. In that world, the bottlenecks are access (can we safely see the docs?) and governance (do we know what this thing did?), not training infrastructure.

We move into “training” when we’re optimizing something: fraud, risk, ranking, pricing, triage, access. There’s labeled data or clear outcome metrics. We care about actual numeric performance and want to tune it over time, not just tweak prompts until it feels okay.

Once the answer is “yes, we are training something,” then there’s a second question: is this an org-wide model or a one-team model? That’s where a central training platform starts to matter.

If the model and features will be reused across many teams, and the data is big, longitudinal, or regulated, I want it on a central training platform with real offline eval and experiment tracking. If it’s a narrow use case, like single product on one team’s data, it’s often fine for that team to own a smaller training stack themselves.

How I think about it:

Training + reused org-wide + big/regulated data → central training platform.
(No training or) Training + narrow + lower stakes → team-owned stack is okay.

A clear example of a model that should be trained and centralized might be a mortality risk prediction model where: (1) it is important to be accurate, (2) it is important to know how accurate it is, and (3) its outputs could be used across multiple groups to understand a population. An example where the edge works fine is an LLM summarizing team meetings.

There are also use cases in the middle, and the goal posts are still moving. One example is copilots that help trained experts, like healthcare providers, search and summarize sensitive data, like clinical data. In many of these cases today, a strong pre-trained LLM with retrieval and some light customization is enough to add value, as long as there is significant expert oversight. But because the data is sensitive and the summaries can subtly shape what people notice or focus on, the risks still need to be evaluated, logged, and revisited as the tool becomes more embedded in care.

Once I know whether and how we’re training, there’s a separate question: where does this thing actually live at runtime?

Question two: where does this run - platform or edge?

Training is one axis. Runtime and data access is another.

Even if you’re not training anything, you still have to decide: does this belong on the data platform or at the edge at runtime?

I’ve ended up with a 2×2 in my head:

- - 

For most use cases that do require training, the “optimal” setup is to train and govern the model on the platform, then orchestrate and render it at the edge via an API call.

And don’t forget the non-AI/ML part: dashboards and insights

Data platforms are also the backbone for dashboards and insights, from staffing to disease surveillance to population health. This work is SQL, modeling, and data stewardship in service of understanding how the organization is performing.

Generative AI makes this even more important. Dashboards and curated tables are how we check whether AI is helping or hurting, and how we spot disparities, blind spots, and unintended consequences. High-quality, well-modeled data is the substrate for both analytics and AI.

Bad data in, bad data out is just as true for a wait-time chart as it is for a mortality model or an LLM assistant.

So what does this mean for data platforms and data/AI strategy in 2020 vs. today?

If teams can ship useful copilots with a base model and a few connectors, are data platforms less important?

I don’t think so. In 2020, the default was that all AI should go through the data platform so we could train and monitor it. That’s no longer true for every use case. GenAI created a whole category of edge-native tools that run fine without sitting in a warehouse.

At the same time, the number of high-stakes data and AI problems has grown. And the analytics work (e.g., dashboards, operational reporting, population health monitoring) hasn’t gone away. So my conclusion is:

- Keep investing in the platform for cross-org, regulated, high-stakes AI and core analytics/measurement.

- Increase investment in data accessibility outside the platform: better APIs, connectors (MCP, etc.), and clear guardrails so edge tools can plug in safely.

- Continue to treat data quality and governance as non-negotiable inputs to all work, whether it is data science, machine learning or generative AI.

A platform’s role is sharper: it doesn’t need to host every AI tool, but it is accountable for the backbone:

- Curated, high-quality data and semantic models for key domains

- Org-wide analytics and measurement that stitch together data from multiple systems

- Org-wide AI foundations: shared datasets, features, and high-stakes models that need a cross-organization view

- Access, policy, and audit permissions, data contracts, and logs that govern how people and AI use the data

What may not need to be on the platform:

- Every chatbot and assistant.

- Ingesting and modeling every operational system, just in case.

- Being a gatekeeper for anyone who wants to experiment.

So the checklist I use now when someone pitches an AI idea is simple:

- Do we need training at all, or is this prompt + retrieval?

- If we train, is it a one-team model or org-wide and high-stakes?

- At runtime, does it need a global, shared view (platform), or can it live safely at the edge?

If it’s no training, one team, low risk, local and UX-heavy, I’m happy for it to live at the edge as long as it logs what it’s doing. If it’s trained, reused org-wide, and high-stakes, it belongs on an enterprise data platform.

title: Making Sense of Data Science Work in an AI-Native World
description: I wrote this mostly for myself to think through how we should be approaching data science in a world that begins to become more AI-native.
text:
The term “data scientist” was coined in 2008 by DJ Patil to describe a wide range of work involving large data sets, computer programming and statistics. Data scientists dig into messy data to find patterns, build models, and surface insights. This work applies broadly, from setting up A/B tests and optimizing email campaigns, to identifying genetic variants linked to cancer, predicting natural disasters, and figuring out where to route a customer service request. It blends elements from analytics, research science, software engineering, and statistics, often all in one day.

DJ himself noted, “The reason I think [the term ‘data scientist’] has fundamentally taken off is because nobody knows what it means.” That ambiguity turned out to be a strength, as data scientists became the people in the room who could translate ambiguity into action.

Thanks for reading Kimberly’s Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

And it worked! All major tech companies fundamentally rely on data scientists to improve their products and services today. LinkedIn leverages data science to match members to jobs; all news feeds are based on complex multi-objective optimization problems; Uber optimizes ride routing and pricing; Spotify uses data science to personalize playlists and recommend new music based on user behavior.

Initially, data science emerged from the need to handle massive datasets and extract meaningful insights, whether it was decoding cancer genetics or understanding customer preferences. It involved individuals writing code to understand, model, predict, and visualize distributions and correlations. For example, my internship data science starter project was: “If our objective is to increase LinkedIn logins, how can we balance the number of emails sent to maximize clicks without increasing unsubscribes?” It turns out the answer to that one is there is no limit—send away!

No-Code and the Limits of Templatized Analytics

Around the 2020s, “no-code” and “low-code” data science platforms promised to make data science more accessible. They worked okay for prototyping and quick insights, especially for non-technical teams, but struggled when things got complex. I remember trying one for a prototype and spending half my time fighting with the UI, then exporting it to write the real code anyway. Data science doesn’t always templatize well.

The Rise of Generative AI

Now, we are in this new era of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI. LLMs are really good at synthesizing incredibly large amounts of structured and unstructured data to generate natural language responses, often accurately. Given this, how does generative AI affect data science today, and how might it reshape the field five years from now?

Currently, I believe generative AI represents another tool in the broader data science toolkit. A data science-driven understanding of the specific problem and proposed solutions remains key. For example, if the goal is to route customer inquiries efficiently, whether using an LLM or traditional machine learning, the data scientist’s workflow is similar:

- Exploratory analysis of data

- Evaluating the accuracy of the proposed solution

- Analysis of edge cases

- Deployment or A/B testing if the solution seems promising

The main difference today lies in the method of "training." Traditional algorithms usually rely heavily on extensive parameter optimization and carefully managed training/test datasets, while LLMs often rely more on prompt optimization and possibly fewer adjustable parameters. There’s complexity involved in both approaches, so the gap might not be as wide as it seems.

- - 

Still the general shape of data science & AI workflows (Credit: https://medium.com/data-science/data-science-workflow-experiment-tracking-609e649973a3)

The Next 5 Years

But what about five years from now? The landscape might shift a lot. AI agents are still pretty early-stage but are gradually entering production environments. Companies like Salesforce are adding agents into products like Einstein Copilot to help with things like support tickets and sales follow-up inside CRM workflows. Startups like Cognition Labs built Devin, an agent that can plan, write, debug, and ship code on its own. And agents like Manus AI are working toward handling more open-ended, multi-step tasks across different tools and systems, moving closer to more general-purpose AI helpers. These agents rely heavily on structured APIs and interoperability protocols like MCP. Fully autonomous AI agents are not widely deployed yet, but likely will be in the next few years.

How Do We Prepare for This Future?

If that’s where we’re headed, what’s the role of data science and what should we do today to prepare? Even in this more AI-driven future, data scientists will still be needed, though specific skillsets may evolve. The need for people who can interrogate models, evaluate performance, and build reliable prediction systems remains. Understanding behavior patterns, identifying correlations, and testing model behavior across edge cases require strong technical judgment and fluency in both statistical methods and computer programming.

What should we be doing to prepare for this world?

- Stay current: Ensure data scientists keep updating their knowledge of the latest models, techniques, and advancements. As the fastest moving space of technology right now, staying up to date is essential.

- Get good at evaluation: Prioritize developing strong skills in evaluating, interpreting, and improving model performance, regardless of the specific technologies used. AI and data science are fundamentally different from traditional software in that they are not deterministic, and understanding and optimizing response distribution remains critical.

- Invest in interoperability: Lay groundwork now by investing in robust data integration, data quality capabilities, and interoperability protocols. Given that data integration projects typically move slowly, especially in large organizations, it’s critical to anticipate what APIs and MCPs will be needed for AI agents and proactively build them.

- Experiment early: Start identifying test cases and building that muscle. Look for spots where AI agents or models could help with repetitive tasks or decisions, and run small experiments. Try things like customer support routing or internal document summarization. We’ve started testing LLM approaches as alternatives to traditional algorithms for most of our data science and ML use cases. They aren’t typically beating out traditional algorithms for classification problems yet, but they are getting closer.

Putting it All Together 

So what does this mean for how we approach data science going forward? We need folks who are comfortable with roles that change every couple years, who can write code and run statistical tests, and who enjoy continuous learning. When choosing where to invest, think about both the immediate problems and how they relate to the rapidly changing future. At the end of the day, we’re still trying to make sense of messy systems and make better decisions. That hasn’t changed much.

title: America Deserves Good Government Technology
description: What if we directed some of the energy & talent developing new technology like self driving cars to making our government services better?
text:
- - 

An autonomous toaster on my street, about to do its usual 15 second stop at the same random stop.

I watch the third autonomous toaster round my corner, stop in the exact same place for exactly 15 seconds, and then roll on.

A lot of funding has gone into developing this technology. Zoox alone raised $800 million before Amazon acquired it in 2020. Autonomous ride shares have been live in SF for over two years now. They’re on time, clean, and drive extremely well, probably around the 85th percentile of human drivers. As a 5-foot, 95-pound female, they also feel a lot safer, and always stop for the pedestrians. They’ve basically outsourced driving - as there’s a human on speed dial who immediately answers and is ready to take over at any moment.

I’ve come around to the robotaxis. And the toasters as well.

Meanwhile, we have minimal bike lanes, one subway line through San Francisco, and still no high-speed rail. If you asked most people, I don’t think they’d ask for more autonomous vehicles. They’d probably ask for a way to get across the city that doesn’t involve a car at all.

But the toasters just work so well.

What would it look like if we brought that same focus to public services?

What if we built government systems that were just as solid, predictable, and forward leaning as autonomous robot taxis?

We already know how to build for reliability and efficiency and usability. We just need to apply it more to our public services.

Building great public services can be just as cool & will improve the lives of all Americans.

And now for the full video (literally this happens on this street every 5 minutes, all day, every day for the past ~2 years).

title: AI-Assisted Software Development Is Here To Help
description: AI assisted software development is here, it works, and it’s already making coding faster, more accessible, and more enjoyable. It won’t rewrite your roadmap, but it will change how quickly you get there.As with every previous step in the evolution of software development, it is up to humans to apply them — so we can build better digital services, faster and bring more people into the act of building them.
text:
- - 

Margaret Hamilton, a person I admire, stacking code written in Universal Systems Language - a software language I am very glad to never use thanks to more modern & efficient ways of writing software.

Summary

AI assisted software development is here, it works, and it’s already making coding faster, more accessible, and more enjoyable. It won’t rewrite your roadmap, but it will change how quickly you get there.

As with every previous step in the evolution of software development, it is up to humans to apply them — so we can build better digital services, faster and bring more people into the act of building them.

Overview

Software engineering has consistently evolved to become easier — from punch cards to IDEs to Stack Overflow. AI-assisted code development tools are the latest step in that progression, starting with advanced autocomplete systems like GitHub Copilot (launched in 2021). More recently, a second generation of tools has emerged such as Cursor, Windsurf, Devin, and GitHub Copilot Agent Mode. These more ‘agentic’ systems go beyond single-file completions. They can iteratively implement end-to-end features and run commands, with humans fully in charge via code or natural language instructions.

These tools are not magic. They are human-in-the-loop systems designed to help developers write higher-quality code, more quickly. They are also not foolproof. While building a web app from scratch can be 10x faster (yes really 10x) with AI (thanks to an abundance of simple web app training data), these tools can struggle with complex or uncommon functions or tasks. A human with strong technical judgement is still key.

That said, most engineers who’ve used the tools will tell you they make coding much more productive and enjoyable. They reduce time spent on repetitive tasks and help developers operate at the top of their license. Far fewer hours spent scouring the web for that one elusive bug, and more time solving real problems. But what does the data say?

Data-Driven Studies on AI Code Generation Tools

Most existing studies focus on non-agentic v1 tools, as the agentic features are so new. Resoundingly, they show positive impact.

- 26% Increase in Completed Tasks Overall: A randomized control study (my favorite kind!) with over 4,000 developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm found that access to a v1 AI code gen tool resulted in a 26% increase in completed tasks (e.g., code commits, pull requests).

- 55% Faster Completion Time of One Specific Task: In a controlled experiment at GitHub, developers using an AI coding tool finished a coding task 55% faster on average than those without AI assistance.​ The AI-assisted group both saved time and had a slightly higher success rate (78% vs. 70%). As with all structured experiments, this may not reflect all real-world complexity, but it is still a clear productivity signal.

- 6% Reduction in Coding Iteration Time Across Large Google Cohort: Google’s internal rollout of an early-stage ML-based code completion across 10k+ engineers led to a 6% reduction in coding iteration time (i.e., time between test runs).

- 55% Increase in Lines of Code: In a 2023 study, Alibaba reported a 55% increase in lines of code written by developers using an AI coding tool. Junior engineers saw the biggest gains, likely because they were using the tools more frequently. (More lines doesn’t necessarily mean more, higher quality software, so this one may be least connected).

Besides efficiency, developers like the tools. They report positive shifts in experience and satisfaction. In a GitHub survey of over 2,000 developers using AI coding tools

- 60–75% reported feeling more fulfilled with their job

- 73% said the tool helped them stay in the flow of coding

- 87% said it saved them mental effort on repetitive tasks​

Agentic AI-Code Development Tooling: The Next Phase

We’re now entering a new phase where tools don’t just autocomplete code, but collaboratively implement features end-to-end. They can take direction like “Create an API that populates this table” and iteratively executive the task with human feedback. Anecdotally, these tools speed up some workflows by 2–10x, especially frontend development, 0-to-1 projects, and small codebases. In one case study, a frontend re-write that was expected to take 6 months was completed in 1 month with Cursor — a 6x speed-up.

While data is catching up, these tools have been rapidly adopted. Y Combinator reported that 25% of the companies in the latest accelerator batch had over 95% of code written by AI, while noting the importance of technical human review.

Common Concerns and Risks

- Code quality: AI-generated code can include insecure patterns, but so can human-written code. Most software engineers (myself included) aren’t security experts. In practice, AI tools often provide faster feedback and more consistent security suggestions than waiting on formal scans. But of course AI does not replace the need for skilled security review.

- Skill erosion: Is it skill erosion or is it just the next phase of how software is developed? I’ve never written a line of assembly language code, and I don’t think it makes me any less capable. Just like compilers and higher-level languages abstracted away complexity to make it feasible to develop products more quickly than before, AI changes what we focus on but not whether we understand the fundamentals.

Conclusion

AI-assisted development is the new normal. Whether you’re a developer or just technically curious, now is the time to try it for yourself.
